title: The Brightest Room
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 30 of 40
content:
Greg volunteered both of us to repaint the community center.

He did it in front of six people and a woman holding a clipboard, which meant I couldn't even throw a paintbrush at him without witnesses.

"Both?" I said.

He glanced sideways. "I meant to ask."

"Before or after you gave away my Saturday?"

"Somewhere in the middle."

The building had been dark long enough that the windows wore a film of dust. A section of the floor was taped off where the boards had lifted. There were chairs stacked in the hallway and old music stands leaning against a wall. Nobody knew whether the heating bill could be covered all winter.

The clipboard woman, who introduced herself as Pilar, handed us the budget. Volunteers had done what they could. A local donor offered to pay for new lights, but he wanted approval over the program and a say in who was allowed to perform.

"Sounds like a pretty big gift," Greg said.

"It's a purchase," I answered.

Pilar looked relieved that somebody had said it out loud.

At the next meeting, the donor arrived in a clean coat and spoke about restoring pride to the neighborhood. He wasn't unkind. He just wanted to put conditions on every dollar. Youth music nights could continue, he said, as long as performances stayed appropriate and the committee signed off on each artist.

"Who decides appropriate?" I asked.

"The board."

"Who appoints the board?"

"I would have a seat."

Greg leaned back. He usually rescued awkward conversations with a joke, but this time he didn't.

"I was thirteen when somebody told me my music wasn't suitable for a serious stage," he said. "They weren't wrong that it was loud. They were wrong that it meant I didn't deserve to play."

The donor folded his hands. "You need funding."

"We do," Pilar said. "But we need a community center even more."

The meeting ended without a donation. The lights stayed old for another week, and I spent most of the evening wondering whether we had done the right thing.

Greg found me scrubbing paint from my fingernails.

"You think we blew it?" he asked.

"I think I wanted money and didn't want the strings. I didn't like being made to choose."

"Me either."

We worked out a smaller plan with Pilar. Repair the safe rooms first. Open one evening a week. Keep the floor section closed until a qualified inspection. Publish the actual costs on the notice board, including the cost of paying the people doing skilled work. Greg offered a free performance but was careful not to promise somebody else's labor. I took charge of the volunteer schedule after asking each person what they could do.

On the first night, three people showed up to play and two just came to listen. A teenager brought a badly tuned instrument, looking as though someone might laugh. Greg tuned it with them rather than taking it away and playing a dazzling demonstration.

Pilar rearranged the chairs when she noticed a narrow turning space beside the door. A volunteer moved the refreshment table out of the route. We didn't call it a heroic act. We just made the room usable.

Near the end of the night, a gust shook the windows and the lights blinked. Everyone froze.

"Old wiring," Greg said.

"Old wiring we need checked," I corrected.

Pilar added it to the list. We closed the back room until the electrician could inspect it. The concert moved to the safer side of the building, where the sound was smaller and the audience could still hear every word.

After the last visitor left, Greg found me standing in the glow from the streetlamps.

"Hey," he said. "About Saturday."

"Yes?"

"I shouldn't have signed you up."

"No, you shouldn't."

He rubbed the back of his neck. "I figured you'd want to help."

"I did want to help. I also wanted you to ask."

He nodded. "Next time, I ask."

"We can put that on the clipboard."

"Is there a punishment for repeat offenders?"

"Sorting the tangled extension cords."

He winced. "Cruel and unusual."

We laughed. He kissed my cheek, paused, and waited. I turned toward him and kissed him properly. Paint dried on my sleeve; the room still needed a lot of work. Outside, Beach City carried on being itself.

I wasn't looking for a perfect building. I was looking for somewhere people could return without having to earn their place by pretending.

The following week, Pilar posted a revised schedule with a second volunteer lead. My name was on it for the nights I'd actually chosen. Greg's was on the music nights he could make. We each had lives outside the center, and that was part of what made the work sustainable.

bridge_outro: At the Lanternwell's winter gathering, Greg played a song nobody had asked him to make perfect. Katara helped the children hang paper stars; Iroh kept the tea hot; Severus stood near the edge of the crowd and pretended not to recognize the melody by its second refrain. Greg caught me looking at him and waggled his eyebrows until I laughed. Later, when the square emptied, he admitted that being heard without needing to impress anyone still frightened him. We walked to Starwake Pier together. He did not fill the silence with another song. I was grateful he knew I could love the person who remained when the music stopped.
